title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot LLM intent→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes. Using gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation, we applied a preregistered binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Of 1,200 planned paired tasks we completed 1,199 pairs. Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0000000000). The paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.0058381985], bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. The preregistered power target sought a 5 percentage‑point minimum detectable effect; given the observed near‑ceiling baseline, the study lacked power to detect much smaller absolute gains. Representative validator traces and provider audit logs show repair was invoked only three times. Under these controlled emulation and task‑corpus conditions we find no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline; we report artifacts, analytic deviation (Wilcoxon → exact McNemar for binary outcomes), and detailed execution accounting to support reproducible interpretation.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent expressed in natural language into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Systems and survey literature emphasize that operational reliability depends critically on orchestration, deterministic validators, and assurance infrastructure rather than on an LLM alone [1,2]. Generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architectures are a canonical mitigation strategy: an LLM proposes candidate outputs, an automated verifier checks constraints and safety, and an automated repair loop iterates until the candidate satisfies verifier rules [3–5]. Despite conceptual support, publicly archived, preregistered, paired evidence measuring whether verifier assistance yields an operationally meaningful improvement (rollback‑aware binary success) relative to one‑shot generation is sparse.

We address this gap with NetOpsTraceBench: a preregistered, paired, emulator‑grounded study comparing (A) baseline one‑shot NL→config generation and (B) a guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline using the same shared initial candidate. The preregistered research question asked whether a workflow‑centered paired benchmark could produce an objective paired binary success metric that distinguishes verifier‑assisted pipelines from one‑shot generation under the planned topology clusters. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered experimental design and full execution artifacts (study ID rX4f7-1); (2) a paired analysis on 1,199 completed pairs using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator; and (3) transparent reporting of an analytic deviation (final confirmatory test used an exact McNemar test appropriate for paired binary outcomes) and execution accounting that explains why the guarded pipeline rarely required repair.
sections.related_work:
Recent survey and system literature frames LLMs as components inside broader AIOps/NetOps workflows and repeatedly emphasizes that correctness and trustworthiness are properties of the whole orchestration stack (model + verifier + provenance + sandboxed execution), not of the base LLM alone [1,2]. Multiple community reviews urge workflow‑centered evaluation—trace quality, validator interactions, and rollback‑aware metrics—rather than isolated one‑shot QA tests; these reviews motivate reproducible, audit‑ready benchmarks that combine generation, deterministic validation, and emulation [1,2,4].

Concrete verifier‑assisted approaches appear across adjacent domains and NetOps prototypes. Work on NL→formal translations and CTL/specification generation demonstrates generator+verifier loops where formal checks drive iterative repairs; topology‑compilation systems translate high‑level security intent into executable topologies with compliance checks and constraint enforcement [5,6]. Prototype efforts in the configuration space (text→config generators and misconfiguration detectors) and domain‑specific “LLM firewalls” illustrate practical patterns: an LLM proposes a candidate, an automated validator enforces syntactic and semantic constraints, and an orchestrator optionally triggers constrained repair or rejects the proposal [7–10].

Empirical and conceptual studies document LLM failure modes that motivate guarded architectures: hallucination, unit/semantic errors, overconfidence/miscalibration, provenance loss, and prompt‑injection vulnerabilities [11–14]. Prior work shows generate–validate‑repair reduces many syntactic and some semantic errors in constrained settings, but gains depend on task difficulty, verifier strictness, and dataset composition. NetOpsTraceBench was designed to make those dependencies observable by preregistering seeds, deterministic task generation, validator rules, and an emulator‑grounded binary outcome.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand: The study preregistration (rX4f7-1; preregistration SHA‑256 = 77abe8b4...) froze confirmatory hypotheses (H1–H3), inclusion/exclusion rules, seeds, stopping rules, and the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration specified 1,200 paired tasks split into two topology clusters (edge=600, core=600) and prespecified analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1.

Task generation, pipelines, and validators: Tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (schema v1.0) with frozen generation_seed values. The two paired conditions used a shared_initial_candidate generation semantics to isolate verifier and repair effects: baseline recorded the initial candidate and proceeded to parsing/emulation; guarded fed the same candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which either accepted it or (if rejected) could trigger at most one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1). Per preregistration the requested model was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). Deterministic validator diagnostics (validation_before/after, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, repair_applied) were recorded per episode.

Topology‑cluster preregistration and execution disclosure (required revision): The preregistration included a confirmatory topology‑cluster breakdown hypothesis (H3) that planned exploratory paired breakdowns across the two simulated topology clusters. The archived, executed confirmatory analysis, however, contains only the pooled paired analysis that we report here; a per‑cluster confirmatory inference (H3) was not executed and thus is not archived. For transparency: the primary archived artifacts supporting the reported pooled analysis are analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json, and execution/execution_manifest.json (all included in the run artifacts). No per‑cluster contingency tables or per‑cluster confirmatory test outputs were produced by the archived analysis executor; therefore H3 is explicitly unexecuted and no per‑cluster confirmatory claims are made in this manuscript.

Design note on shared_initial_candidate: The shared_initial_candidate paired design was chosen to isolate the verifier/repair mechanism by removing independent generation variability between conditions. This design reduces noise attributable to stochastic generation but has the operational consequence of reducing repair invocation frequency when initial candidates already satisfy deterministic validator rules; archived stage_counts and repair counts (repair = 3) corroborate that effect.
sections.results:
Execution summary and accounting: The run completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes producing 1,199 complete paired observations (complete_pair_count = 1,199; failed_episode_count = 2). Provider audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203 (completed = 1,202; failed = 1); stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 1,200; repair = 3 (execution/execution_manifest.json).

Primary paired outcomes (pooled): The archived contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 1,196, n10 = 3, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline_success_count = 1,196/1,199 = 0.9974979149; guarded_success_count = 1,199/1,199 = 1.0. Paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002502085070892446. The confirmatory analysis executed an exact McNemar two‑sided test (archived) giving p = 0.25. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000) is [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957] (analysis/results.json and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).

Missingness, repairs, and representative traces: Missingness summary (analysis/missingness_summary.csv) reports complete_pairs = 1,199; failed_baseline_episodes = 1; failed_guarded_episodes = 1; both_missing_pairs = 1. Repair-stage calls were recorded for exactly three episodes; representative scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task-000213-*/, execution/scoring/task-000333-*/, execution/scoring/task-000941-*/) show the three discordant pairs where the guarded pipeline invoked repair and converted baseline failures into guarded successes (terminal_factual_accounting lists these pair identifiers). Representative per-episode JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) archived validator_trace fields (validation_before/after.valid and repair_applied) that underpin the binary success scoring.

Interpretation constrained by pooled execution: The pooled analysis shows all discordant pairs favored the guarded pipeline (n10 = 3, n01 = 0) but the absolute discordant count is too small to meet preregistered inferential thresholds. As stated above, the preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory test H3 was not executed; therefore the manuscript does not report nor claim per‑cluster confirmatory results.
sections.discussion:
Statistical and operational interpretation: The pooled exact McNemar test and bootstrap CI indicate no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline under the executed corpus and validator configuration (p = 0.25; CI includes zero). Two artifact‑grounded explanations are supported by archived evidence. First, the observed near‑ceiling baseline (≈99.75%) left little headroom for absolute improvement; the preregistered MDE was 5 percentage points, so the run was not powered to detect the observed ≈0.25 percentage‑point effect. Second, the shared_initial_candidate design combined with deterministic synthetic tasks and a validator configuration that enforces explicit required_sequence constraints led initial candidates to satisfy validator checks in the majority of episodes, so repair was rarely invoked (repair = 3). Both points are evidenced in the deterministic_reconciliation and execution/execution_manifest artifacts.

Threats to validity and externality: Internal validity is strengthened by deterministic seeds, frozen task generation, and automated exclusion rules. Construct validity depends on whether the binary success rule (validator acceptance + emulator availability tolerance + no rollback) corresponds to operational correctness across production contexts. External validity is limited: a single requested model family (gpt-5-mini) was used, the task corpus is synthetic/consented and vendor‑agnostic, and emulation may not capture vendor idiosyncrasies and routing convergence phenomena. Conclusion validity: low discordant counts imply limited power to detect small absolute differences; the preregistered MDE should be considered when interpreting the null result.

Operational implications and next steps: Under conditions where initial generation commonly satisfies deterministic validator criteria, verifier scaffolding will be infrequently exercised and measured gains on a binary success metric will be small. To evaluate verifier value more sensitively, future work should (a) expand task ambiguity/adversariality, (b) vary verifier strictness, (c) perform per‑cluster confirmatory analyses when planned and archived, and (d) test multiple model families. The archived artifacts included with this run provide exact seeds, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis code to enable such sensitivity studies.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench (rX4f7-1), a paired, emulator‑grounded study comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted NL→configuration pipelines. On 1,199 completed pairs under deterministic synthetic tasks and the requested gpt-5-mini configuration, baseline one‑shot generation achieved near‑ceiling success (≈99.75%). The guarded pipeline improved absolute success by ≈0.25 percentage points (paired difference = 0.0025020851) but this small discordant count (n10 = 3, n01 = 0) produced exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25 and a 95% bootstrap CI including zero. Crucially, the preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis (H3) was not executed and no per‑cluster confirmatory results are archived; the reported inferential results are pooled across clusters and supported by the archived artifacts analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json, and execution/execution_manifest.json. We emphasize that the observed null result reflects limited headroom given task and validator choices rather than definitive evidence that verifiers are never useful; follow‑up sensitivity studies using the archived artifacts are recommended.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary. This deviation is recorded in the archived analysis artifacts and in the Disclosure Statement above.
Operational external validity: absence of heterogeneous vendor renderers, real production templates, and live rollouts constrain direct production generalization.
